physicalNotes: Radius 2.610 +/- 0.087 Earth radii from Benneke et al. (2019, ApJL 887, L14; arXiv:1909.04642), Table 1, at 6378.137 km per Earth radius. GM from the mass 8.63 +/- 1.35 Earth masses Benneke et al. list from Cloutier et al. (2019, A&A 621, A49), times Earth's GM 398600.4418 km^3/s^2. A sphere: no oblateness is measured.

sources.period: Benneke et al. (2019, ApJL 887, L14; arXiv:1909.04642), Table 1: 32.940045 +/- 0.000010 d. Measured here, eight JWST transits of 2023-2025 (programmes 2722 and 2372, MAST white-light curves, trapezoid fits) fall 8.5 to 12.0 minutes before this ephemeris, drifting about 3 minutes over 26 orbits; the drift is not drawn.
sources.shape: Benneke et al. (2019, ApJL 887, L14; arXiv:1909.04642), Table 1: a = 0.15910 au and R* = 0.4445 solar radii give a/R* = 76.97; impact parameter b = 0.641 gives inclination 89.5228 degrees (circular geometry: with this record's eccentricity the inclination differs by about 0.01 degrees).
sources.phase: Benneke et al. (2019, ApJL 887, L14; arXiv:1909.04642), Table 1: T0 = BJD_UTC 2457725.551189, the time of inferior conjunction, here BMJD_TDB 57725.05199 (TT - UTC = 69.184 s).
sources.orientation: Display convention: transit photometry does not measure the orbit's position angle on the sky, so the ascending node is set at position angle 0 (celestial north).
sources.eccentricity: Sarkis et al. (2018, AJ 155, 257; arXiv:1805.00830), Table 3 (joint HARPS and CARMENES-VIS radial velocities): e = 0.20 +/- 0.08.
sources.argumentOfPeriapsis: Sarkis et al. (2018), Table 3: omega = -0.10 (+0.81/-0.59) rad, fitted with RadVel, whose transit convention f = pi/2 - omega is the one this record uses; here 354.27 degrees.
